The lost tug of war with Sunderland over Malick Fofana summed up another chaotic deadline day for Palace, who were still scrambling for signings in the final minutes and confirmed the arrivals of Ben Chilwell, Quinten Timber and Darío Osorio after the window shut. The new manager, Pierre Sage, will at least be pleased to have secured more defensive reinforcements after losing Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea, with the loanees Honest Ahanor and Axel Disasi adding much-needed depth. Palace also kept hold of Ismaïla Sarr – presuming he doesn’t join a club in Saudi Arabia before the Sunday deadline there – after rejecting an approach from Liverpool for the Senegal forward. EA

Key ins: Anan Khalaili (Union St-Gilloise, £21m), Quinten Timber (Marseille, £15m), Zavier Gozo (Real Salt Lake, £11m), Axel Disasi (Chelsea, loan), Evann Guessand (Aston Villa, loan), Honest Ahanor (Atalanta, loan), Darío Osorio (Midtjylland, loan), Dwight McNeil (Everton, swap), Takehiro Tomiyasu (Ajax, free), Óscar Mingueza (Celta Vigo, free), Ben Chilwell (Strasbourg, undisclosed fee)

Key outs: Maxence Lacroix (Chelsea, £52m), Daniel Muñoz (Nottingham Forest, £22m), Brennan Johnson (Everton, swap), Borna Sosa (Cologne, loan)

It was a window that revealed the extent of The Friedkin Group’s ambitions, the strength of the club’s finances after the move to a new stadium, the state of the relationship between the manager and chief executive and the expertise of the senior leadership team; and none of it was positive. The owners deserve some credit for listening to fans and halting the self-defeating sale of Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest but otherwise it was a modest window that descended into a shambles. The club’s best player was sold for a below-market fee, a move for Folarin Balogun collapsed and although the equally desperate search for a right-back ended with Ainsley Maitland-Niles signing, David Moyes was left with one striker and a smaller squad than he started the day with, despite repeatedly urging his employers to strengthen. AH

It was a summer of change at Craven Cottage. Marco Silva departed after five successful years in charge and was replaced by the inexperienced Álvaro Arbeloa, who has focused on adding youth. Gonzalo García, César Palacios and Manuel Ángel followed Arbeloa from Real Madrid and Shea Charles is an exciting signing from Southampton. Some stalwarts have left. Raúl Jiménez joined Wolves and Harry Wilson went to Leeds. Fulham looked to strengthen. “Think of us like a volcano,” said Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali, in early July. “It’s boiling right now and it’s going to erupt.” Two months on the Ilicali has presided over 18 signings, investing more than £150m and his manager, Sergej Jakirovic, has choreographed two Premier League wins. The horizon looks infinitely brighter than in June, when the playoff winners sold two players for a combined £8.5m to avoid breaching English Football League spending rules and a near-certain six-point deduction. Hull, remember, spent last season under a two-window EFL transfer embargo. They have compensated for that this summer and, although time will tell whether all those new faces are compatible, reasons for optimism remain real. Not least because last season’s cult hero loanee forward Joe Gelhardt has signed permanently from Leeds. Louise Taylor

Arrivals such as Exequiel Palacios and Julio Enciso should have no business in the lower reaches, and the former Fulham pair Sasa Lukic and Issa Diop add crucial experience. #885. Why Man Utd's Roma comeback has echoes of Mourinho and Solskjaer

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick (second left) hugs Shea Lacey after the 3-2 Champions League victory against Roma

It was impossible not to get swept up in the emotion and delirium of Manchester United's late 3-2 Champions League comeback win against Roma.

Old Trafford was transformed from a mutinous, baying cathedral of distrust and fury to one of joy and celebration.

Nine games and almost eight weeks is an eternity to wait for a victory at a club of Manchester United's size.

It didn't take Michael Carrick long to calm the mood.

"It's one win, so we're not getting too carried away with things, but it was an important win."

It was a huge result in the sense it bought Carrick some time. But given United's general state, no-one can be sure how much.

And, as was quickly pointed out in the aftermath of the victory, Manchester United have been here before.

Man Utd produce incredible second-half comeback to beat Roma

A half-time speech, a retaken penalty - and a win to save Carrick's job?

Jose Mourinho (centre) was sacked after a 3-1 defeat at Liverpool in December 2018

'Jose Mourinho set to be sacked whatever Manchester United's result vs Newcastle.'

As headlines go, it was attention grabbing.

As it turned out, the Mirror was wrong. Although United officials at the time tried to play down the situation, sources have since admitted the intention was to sack Mourinho after presiding over the club's worst start to a season in 29 years, and defeat by Newcastle would make it inevitable.

Much like the Roma game, the visitors raced into a two-goal lead and the atmosphere in the stadium started to turn, with most of the venom aimed at the director's box rather than the manager.

Mourinho, who had promoted Carrick to assistant coach, replaced Eric Bailly with Juan Mata after 19 minutes and it was Mata who scored the 70th-minute goal that sparked the comeback, completed by Alexis Sanchez in the final minute for a 3-2 victory.

After the game, Mourinho said the pressure on him was a "manhunt". However, the relationship between manager and club had been turning sour since the previous summer. His demand for Anthony Martial to be sold had been rejected, while record signing Paul Pogba was proving a problem.

While the Newcastle win sparked an improvement in form, a run of two wins in eight games culminating in a 3-1 loss at Liverpool led to Mourinho's dismissal 10 weeks later.

Former United defender Rio Ferdinand dismissed calls for Ole Gunnar Solskjaer to be sacked before the Champions League encounter with Atalanta on 20 October 2021 as representative of "current fan culture".

Carrick was also part of Solskjaer's coaching group as United went top of the Premier League when they beat Newcastle just over a month earlier, but two wins in seven suggested all was not well.

As he did with Roma, coach Gian Piero Gasperini saw his team establish a two-goal lead by half-time, then collapse. Cristiano Ronaldo was the matchwinner on this occasion, nine minutes from time for another 3-2 win.

Even if United had lost that night, it is hard to think Solskjaer's job would have been under threat. What followed immediately afterwards was a totally different story.

Liverpool came to Old Trafford and established a four-goal first-half lead. Jurgen Klopp's men won 5-0, their biggest ever away win over their old rivals.

Many United fans thought Solskjaer should go that night. It was three weeks later that it happened, after a 4-1 defeat at Watford.

Man Utd beat Roma - the other great Champions League comebacks

Fernandes critical of media 'lies' about Carrick relationship

Manchester United skipper Bruno Fernandes celebrates Matheus Cunha's winner against Roma

One look at the Premier League table shows why Carrick is right not to get carried away.

If results go against them, Manchester United could be bottom of the table by the time they kick-off against Aston Villa on Sunday.

Neither Mourinho nor Solskjaer could follow up their 3-2 successes with another victory. Mourinho's United drew at Chelsea, then lost at home to Juventus. Solskjaer's United were embarrassed by Liverpool. It meant neither man was able to build on the momentum generated by their epic victories.

United have gone seven Premier League games without a win. They went eight under Ruben Amorim at the end of the 2024-25 campaign, but draws and losses were split by victories en route to the Europa League final, so the effect was not as great as it feels right now.

The club does have an exceptional home record against Villa. They have won their past six in all competitions and lost just two league games against the Midlands outfit at Old Trafford since 1983.

When United sources finally communicated - almost 48 hours after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October - that Carrick and his players would be given the opportunity to turn the situation around, no timescale was put on this. However, the feeling was the forthcoming international break would be an appropriate time for the club hierarchy to take stock and decide what direction they should go in.

In the two games since, Carrick's team have been excellent across two halves.

Victory against Villa, albeit with Â£70m Carlos Baleba joining the injured list, would haul them up to within two points of Unai Emery's side heading into a tricky run of matches post international break, starting at Liverpool, but also including trips to Newcastle and Arsenal in December.

Defeat is likely to dump them in the relegation zone for at least a fortnight and facing severe baiting at Anfield on 22 November.

"It's not about me," is a phrase Carrick has repeated often as he has assessed the wreckage of another bad result. The outcome against Roma was much more positive.

There is no suggestion Carrick's future has been decided just yet. What happens at Old Trafford this weekend looks very important.

#883. Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?

After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Bart Verbruggen (Brighton): He was unreal. Lots of saves which kept Brighton in it at Manchester City, even the last-ditch stop where it hit him in the face.

Just an impenetrable wall. Brighton should really have lost by two or three goals, but Verbruggen was the reason they managed to hold on for a 1-0 win.

Archie Gray (Tottenham): I'm going with a fully north London back four. Gray scored and defended really well against Crystal Palace. He was under a lot of pressure when Tottenham were in bad form and got a lot of stick, but now Spurs are starting to pick up I'm going to give him a bit of credit.

Ezri Konsa (Arsenal): He was a beast in Arsenal's 1-0 win at Anfield. Head it, kick it, throw your body in front of the ball. He defended and fought for the team, getting the job done.

Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham): Van Hecke got a goal and he's really growing into his role at Spurs. I still think he was a little bit overpriced, but all in all he's had a solid start, coming up with a few goals. Micky van de Ven next to him gives him confidence that he can go and be really aggressive, because Van der Ven will cover him with his pace.

Jurrien Timber (Arsenal): Timber got away with a shirt pull on Alexander Isak and I'm really surprised the referee and video assistant referee (VAR) didn't look at it. But I thought he recovered and defended really well at full-back.

Romeo Lavia (Chelsea): I thought Lavia was excellent for Chelsea. People will turn to Manchester United having 10 men, but the 60 minutes before that Chelsea were all over the place. Lavia was the only constant breaking up play, keeping the ball moving. Plus he had an assist.

Declan Rice (Arsenal): A proper captain's performance, he gets the job done all over the pitch. He got a little assist for himself, too.

Tatsuhiro Sakamoto (Coventry): Sakamoto goes unnoticed by a lot of people, but I think he works really hard for the team and he is very humble in his approach. On Saturday he also delivered in a massive win for his team against Sunderland.

Johan Manzambi (Aston Villa): Another assist for the 21-year-old who is just flying. His confidence is through the roof and he is taking over this Villa team. Really good player, only going to get better. He was taken off thinking about the Champions League game against Barcelona, but up until that point Fulham couldn't really stop him.

Ollie McBurnie (Hull): Grafter, scrappy, endeavour, goals, assists... he had it all in his game in the draw against Ipswich.

He epitomises what Hull are: a player that's always overlooked, a team that's always overlooked, but they've got some spirit and some fight.

Taiwo Awoniyi (Coventry): Unbelievable solo goal. It's really good to see the big fella back playing and being in a situation where he can impose himself. If Coventry are to stay up, he's going to be why.

Frank Lampard (Coventry): He has been really good. Coventry have taken care of business against Sunderland, it was a massive six-pointer and his team came out front-footed, aggressive and also did a job on a very good Sunderland team.

Also a massive nod to Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta for getting the job done at Liverpool.

#882. John Mulaney Reveals Parenting Hack for Teaching Son to Ride a Bike

Madden star John Mulaney revealed to E! News the unusual way that he taught his and Olivia Munn's 4-year-old son Malcolm how to ride a bike.

And after nearly five years as a dad under his belt, the training weeks are certainly off when it comes to parenthood—especially around the holidays. In fact, the Everybody's Live with John Mulaney host is really looking forward" to the upcoming holiday season, which is also when his son will celebrate his birthday.

"He's gonna be 5," he shared. "My son has his demands, but he's very good at communicating them. If I say, 'You seem really frustrated about this,' he can kinda collect himself and say, 'I just want you to leave, because Mama will let me watch more TV.' And I go, 'OK, so you don't hate me, I just won't let you watch Duggee,' or whatever the hell."

Mulaney also shared why he took on the role of Electronic Arts founder Trip Hawkins in Madden, which tells the story of John Madden and the eponymous video game empire he spawned.

"What's funny about the game itself—and this is touched on in the movie, but this was really true in the way they looked at it," he said. "This sounds like wishful thinking, but they kind of they realized the game would make kids want to play football and go outside."

#877. Meet the people set for key role in deciding Man City fate

Manchester City have been sponsored by Etihad since May 2009

They are the five individuals at the Premier League set to play a key role in the fate of Manchester City.

The competition's board has the responsibility of recommending a punishment after the seismic news in September of the club being found guilty of breaching financial rules by an independent commission.

While that three-person commission panel will ultimately decide on a sanction, the Premier League's submission will be considered, along with the view of City of course, who maintain their innocence and have appealed.

It is not known when a sanction hearing will take place, nor what sanction the Premier League will want for what it describes as the most significant disciplinary case in its history, with a fine, points deduction, expulsion or the stripping of past titles all possible.

So who makes up the Premier League's board, and how have their recommendations over punishments been received in past disciplinary cases?

Among various roles and responsibilities, the board is the entity responsible for prosecuting breaches of Premier League rules.

It comprises the league's chair, chief executive, and three independent non-executive directors, with no club representatives included - in order to provide independence and neutrality.

Do Manchester City have any grounds to win their appeal?

How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?

Alison Brittain has kept a low profile since becoming the league's first female chair almost four years ago. Formerly a senior executive in the hospitality and financial services sectors, she is also chair and trustee of The King's Trust Group.

Described as "sensible" by one acquaintance, in September she spoke at a university event, revealing that she was initially sceptical about joining the Premier League because she had never worked in sport.

Two senior club executives - the former Arsenal CEO Vinai Venkatesham (now at Spurs), and ex-Aston Villa CEO Christian Purslow - told her that her skillset was what the league needed, helping to persuade her to apply.

She said: "They actually spent some time talking to me and saying 'we aren't looking for a super fan. In fact we're looking for the exact opposite - somebody who will bring a different mindset. A business mindset, governance standards, be able to reset us a little bit into a different way'â¦and so I then went through the process and ended up in the job."

Describing herself as a "lifelong Manchester United fan [who] stood in the Stretford End before it had seats, as a kid" because of her family's allegiance, Brittain is now also a Brentford supporter. In 2025, she received unanimous backing from the 20 clubs to continue for a second three-year stint.

Speaking in 2024, Brittain acknowledged the league was "not without its challenges". But she has hailed what she describes as "the most exciting competition in the world", and its global appeal, calling it an "enormous soft power asset" for the country.

She also recently said that "the whole point of running the league... is to make sure the competitive balance stays really good. Because what makes us successful is this virtuous circle of anyone could win any match any dayâ¦ there has to be jeopardy."

She added: "Someone has to care about keeping that balance, because if you ask the clubs they'd rather not have that balance because they'd like to win all the time."

When asked if that was her job, she replied: "Absolutely. That's my job."

According to Purslow, Brittain has "extremely good people skills and diplomacy in a role where keeping 20 owners more or less happy is not an easy job. She is a very down to earth, straightforward person, and that plays well."

Richard Masters has been the Premier League's chief executive since 2019

The league's chief executive since 2019, Richard Masters is a much more familiar face to football fans.

When the independent commission's 'core decision' on City was announced in September, he said it "vindicates the Premier League's decision to pursue this case", and that the league has "a key responsibilityâ¦ to ensure that the rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition".

He added that it was "paramount that the league remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously."

Masters said: "There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the commission's decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the league, our clubs and fans."

Reportedly having grown up an Aston Villa fan, in 2024 Masters assured a parliamentary committee that "the Premier League board applies the rules consistently, irrespective of the club in question".

The board is completed with three other directors:

Mai Fyfield - a former Sky executive who during her 20-year career at the company led its bidding for three Premier League TV cycles, and currently sits on the board of BBC Commercial.

Dharmash Mistry - a technology venture capitalist and entrepreneur who also has experience of working with the BBC as a former non-executive director at the corporation. Mistry is "smart and theoretical" according to one colleague. He chairs the Premier League's audit and finance committee and is its representative on the FA's board.

Matthew Ryder - a senior barrister, part-time judge and a former deputy mayor of London when he had responsibility for social mobility and social engagement. He is also a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian newspaper, alongside other non-executive roles. Describing himself as "a longstanding and passionate football fan", he also chairs the league's legal advisory group. He told a conference last year that his membership of the Premier League board had been "deeply rewarding... it's a fascinating time to be in football."

BBC Sport has approached the board members via the Premier League, but it declined to comment.

How did Man City's 'disguised funding scheme' work?

The Manchester City case is unique in its scale, and so it is uncertain how relevant previous cases are when looking at the kind of sanctions the Premier League has recommended. But it is clear that independent commissions do not necessarily agree with the Premier League's board when it comes to clubs' potential punishments.

In 2023, the league argued for a 12-point sanction for Everton after the club breached financial rules, with a commission then settling on a 10-point punishment instead, which was reduced to six points on appeal.

In 2024, the Premier League suggested that Nottingham Forest should be docked eight points over a larger PSR overspend, but the commission again disagreed, settling on a four-point punishment.

This year the Premier League argued that an appropriate sanction for Leicester City - for an overspend in 2023-24 - was a 12-point deduction to be applied in the Championship. The independent commission instead recommended that a six-point deduction be imposed by the EFL.

There is also an alternative to contested proceedings.

Earlier this year the Premier League board reached a 'sanctions agreement' with Chelsea which resulted in a Â£10m fine and suspended transfer ban after admitting making Â£47m in secret payments to unregistered agents and third parties over transfers between 2011 and 2018.

The league said: "When considering the appropriate sanction, the board noted that the club's proactive self-reporting, admissions of breach and exceptional co-operation throughout the investigation acted as significant mitigating factors."

#876. Mainoo and Lacey raise the spirits but systemic change still required at Manchester United | Nick Ames

There were protests at Old Trafford and even though two academy products stood out, Michael Carrick’s future is far from safe

Green and yellow balloons bobbed around the Stretford End. Tennis balls rained down on the pitch in protest at the chronic, enduringly cinematic decline presided over by Manchester United’s ownership. Then came a reminder of the humble football’s extraordinary power to bend history, minds and wills. United’s players departed victorious having somehow won the game within the game, separating themselves from the fog of unhappy context swirling on all sides and turning the second half into its own soaring, ripping story for the ages.

Will it be enough to save Michael Carrick, who was once again serenaded when minds wandered from the joint scourges of the Glazer family and Jim Ratcliffe? If Aston Villa defend a shade more competently than Roma on Sunday then perhaps not. United have led their supporters, remarkable in their tenor of backing for players and head coach here, up more than enough false peaks over the past 13 years. Arguably, that is one reason for Carrick being given the job on a permanent basis.

Until United are equipped to repeat their second 45 minutes on a weekly basis, which requires systemic change in departments far outside the technical area, even if Carrick’s head will surely be first on the block, nobody is likely to deliver them from ongoing psychodrama. History may tell that his heavily maligned players were fruitlessly raging against the dying of the light in blowing Roma out of the water. But their achievement here was worth savouring for its discrete brilliance and, perhaps, the wholesome powers that ultimately wrought it.

Kobbie Mainoo had been introduced as “Manchester born and bred”, to obligatory cheers, when the teams were read out. Any emotional heartstring is worth plucking on at the moment but there was something grounding about seeing the midfielder, largely injured over the past month and an onlooker while his colleagues’ fortunes spiralled, return to the starting XI. Mainoo was far from alone in enduring a tentative, twitchy, flustered first half but was caught flat-footed when Marten de Roon mugged him near halfway, setting in train the move that exposed an execrably organised backline for Matías Soulé’s opener.

At 2-0, another crossfield ball from the left having triggered United’s defence into recidivism, Mainoo attempted to raise spirits by surging through the middle on his own and spraying the ball right under pressure. There was no more nourishing gruel on offer than this; the only nagging glimmer of possibility was that Roma, for all their broad control, did not look like the kind of side that would withstand any gale that came their way.

When Carlos Baleba, eye-catching in phases but loose in possession, pulled up with Bryan Mbeumo ready for a tap-in, the notes of misery deepened. But the subsequent introduction of Youri Tielemans, in his element against opponents whose intensity was evidently sagging, created angles and spaces that had previously seemed figments of the mind. United were fortunate when Bruno Fernandes converted his soft, twice-taken penalty; they were presented with parity when Leonardo Balerdi’s air-kick afforded Matheus Cunha a chance he could barely miss. The die, though, had long been cast through their waves of slick, insistent pressure.

So it fell for Mainoo and another academy product, Shea Lacey, to tee up the coup de grace. Lacey hails from Liverpool but there is no need to whisper that: his credentials since childhood have firmly passed muster. While Lisandro Martínez was lightly booed on to the pitch in the 75th minute, Lacey arrived with him to raptures. How poetic it was that Mainoo, speeding up an attack before quickly shifting the ball right, and the mesmerising Lacey, should complete the revival.

Lacey’s jink inside and left-footed pass whipped into Cunha were genuinely breathtaking. So was the finish and so, too, the reaction. Few do it quite like an Old Trafford crowd on a European night. This is still a citadel like no other, even if its strains nowadays alternate between dubbing Mainoo unplayable and impolitely requesting the Glazers to make haste back across the Atlantic.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The contradictions fizzed everywhere on this thick, still night. Earlier on Wednesday Carrick will doubtless have been spared the news that sacking season had already visited the Ineos football empire. At this point Jim Ratcliffe’s sporting citadels are more akin to a line of Dickensian rubbish heaps, their proprietor a modern-day golden dustman, and the plug had been pulled on Luka Elsner and United’s hapless junior sibling, Lausanne Sport. They are bottom of the Swiss top flight and results, a club statement explained, had been the determining factor in the manager’s demise.

They have not exactly helped Carrick either. Mainoo had claimed in a transactionally toned pre-match press conference that United could be “one win away” from changing the shape and scope of their season. In reality all that can be guaranteed about whatever occurs next is the sheer theatre of it. Of course it is Unai Emery, discussion whose suitability or otherwise for any United vacancy has brought surprising ramifications, who walks into this perplexing cocktail of loathing and unconditional support this weekend. Carrick will need the football to perform him a few more favours yet.

#875. What new Kane deal means for England and the Premier League record

England captain Harry Kane scored scored 213 times in 320 league games for Tottenham

Harry Kane's decision to sign a new contract with Bayern Munich carries heavy significance for the Bundesliga giants, who have been celebrating his status as a Ballon d'Or winner, but also for England and the Premier League's record books.

Bayern have acted swiftly to secure the 33-year-old on a deal taking him through to 2029 after he was crowned the world's best player, ensuring England's captain and record goalscorer will spend the final peak years of a magnificent career at Allianz Arena.

Kane has written himself into Bayern legend since joining from Spurs for Â£86m in August 2023, scoring 102 goals in 102 Bundesliga matches, winning two league titles and three successive Golden Boot awards.

It is why Bayern could not contemplate his departure as other clubs eyed his next move - and why the announcement Kane is staying casts ripples far beyond Munich.

Does it mean Kane will never grace the Premier League again? And does it mean - far more enticingly - he has his sights set on two more major tournaments and two more chances to grasp the prize that has eluded him at international level?

Former England striker Chris Sutton told BBC Sport: "I certainly think, although you always have to factor fitness issues into all of this, that Harry is more than capable of carrying on for a few years yet, easily.

"People might say his game lacks a little bit of pace, but he's so strong in other areas. He is a world-class all-round player. His finishing isn't going to be affected in any way by his age. He can still link up play and his football brain is first class.

"I don't see his age being such a big deal. You think of pacy players over the years who rely on that part of the game then lose it as they get older. Harry is not one of those. He seems fit and at the peak of his powers with Bayern and England."

Kane's new contract expires shortly before his 36th birthday, certainly raising the prospect the player who left Spurs as the highest scorer in their history with 280 goals in 435 appearances may never grace the Premier League again.

His consummate professionalism, and apparent ability to develop into the complete player with age, means this can never be discounted.

The notion of an emotional return to Spurs at some point has often provided background noise, but now looks increasingly unlikely.

What it surely means is that Alan Shearer will remain the Premier League's highest scorer - who knows what will happen with Erling Haaland as Manchester City await punishment after being found guilty of breaching financial regulations they deny? - and out of Kane's reach.

Harry Kane won the Ballon d'Or after 73 goals in 65 games for Bayern Munich and England during the 2025â26 season

Shearer scored 260 goals in 441 Premier League matches for Blackburn Rovers and Newcastle United. Kane scored 213 times in 320 league games for Spurs.

With Kane still 47 short of Shearer's record, it would need a spectacular late-career flourish for him to eclipse the Geordie icon's tally to write another entry into the history books, which also have him as England's highest scorer with 91 goals from a record-equalling 125 caps.

What will be of huge interest to Thomas Tuchel - the coach who took him to Bayern and now leads England - is that Kane has delivered a clear indication that Euro 2028, to be played in the UK and Ireland, is firmly in his sights.

And, when this new deal expires, Kane is also only a year away from the 2030 World Cup, to be played in Morocco, Portugal and Spain, with special centenary opening matches held in Uruguay, Argentina, and Paraguay.

This, of course, is a stretch given the inevitable rigours of age, but few who know Kane, who have watched him move to a new level at Bayern, would ever say never to such a driven personality, hiding fierce mental strength and a competitive instinct behind his humble 'anti-superstar' persona.

Sutton said: "Euro 2028 certainly shouldn't be a problem and who knows beyond that? If Harry has got players around him with pace and dynamism, as well as runners in and around him, then his football brain isn't going to change and he can still play a huge part.

"He's such a sharp, quick, thinker. He reads the game superbly, knows where his next pass is going and has shown an ability to drop deep and impact the game.

"Harry just seems to be getting better and more rounded with age. And as for age, just look at someone like Teddy Sheringham. He was playing and scoring goals for West Ham United in the Premier League in his 40s.

"Sheringham was an incredibly talented player with supreme intelligence. Harry Kane falls right into the same category.

"Ronaldo has just retired from international football with Portugal at 41, but he is a totally different player than Harry Kane. Harry is one who can drop a little bit deeper to use his incredible ability and range of passing.

"As well as that ability, it is about how Harry's football brain works as much as anything and that won't change with age."

'My heart was beating so fast' - Kane wins Ballon D'or

And it is an argument, and a hope, that is even more pertinent as England still do not possess any other striker or forward who could be considered anywhere near Kane's class or potency.

"When you talk about 2028 or 2030, who are the English strikers coming through to challenge him to take him out of the team?" said Sutton. "There's no-one in his class or effectiveness, or anywhere near it."

What also plays into the argument that Kane cannot be ruled out of such long-term involvement is the manner in which he responded so superbly to what was a disappointing Euro 2024, not only as England lost in the final to Spain but because he looked a jaded shadow of his old self.

Kane looked so out of sorts there was a clamour for him to be replaced by Ollie Watkins, then at Aston Villa. He was substituted in all of England's knockout matches, including after only 61 minutes of that final loss to Spain in Berlin.

And yet, Kane still finished as the tournament's joint top scorer with three goals from seven games.

The notion of him being replaced with the stakes so high now is unthinkable, such is his peerless form and stature.

While Bayern are convinced their new investment in Kane's brilliance will be rewarded with further honours, Tuchel will hope it is motivation and inspiration to finally end the country's long wait for international glory.

#874. West Ham took too long to sack Nuno and now must trust Parker to do what he does best | Jacob Steinberg

Forget speculation over how a Parker-led side would fare in the Premier League and let the man who has taken three clubs up do his work again

It has taken West Ham six months to come to their senses and sack Nuno Espírito Santo, but at least the decision has arrived early enough to revive their hopes of automatic promotion.

Dithering was no longer an option after the dismal performance against West Brom last Saturday.

West Ham, eighth in the Championship and four points off the top two, had to act after a second consecutive home defeat. They are in danger of slipping into a battle for a playoff spot and needed to move on from Nuno after just over a year of his confused, passive football.

Nuno did a terrible job after replacing Graham Potter as manager in September 2025. The 52-year-old had 33 games to save West Ham from relegation and failed. He has the most expensive squad in the Championship but his side have not lived up to their billing as title favourites and their stuttering form has exposed the folly of not sacking Nuno at the end of last season.

David Sullivan, then the club’s largest shareholder, wanted a change. But Daniel Kretinsky favoured continuity and looked to capitalise on the shifting power dynamics in the boardroom. Karren Brady had stepped down as vice-chair in April – Karim Virani replaced her in an interim role – and there was further upheaval when Sullivan resigned as joint-chair and a director of the club to fight what he described as “false allegations” regarding his personal conduct.

Sullivan bears most culpability for West Ham’s relegation. He still owns a 40% stake but is no longer on the board and West Ham are better off without him dictating key decisions. Equally, though, where Sullivan was not mistaken was in wanting Nuno gone. Kretinsky got his first big call wrong. At least the Czech billionaire has given Nuno’s replacement time to get the team back on track. The task falls to Scott Parker, who has been on the market since leaving Burnley last April. Parker is regarded as a “safe” appointment and has been on West Ham’s radar for a while.

Some wanted the former England midfielder in the summer and his name was mentioned again when West Ham failed to win their first three league games. Patience was wearing thin. A subsequent run of four wins in a row swiftly proved a false dawn.

West Ham have not had the right mindset. They have two wins from their past six games and have often started playing only after going a goal down. A 6-0 win against Wrexham was a highlight but victory at Lincoln by the same scoreline came with the caveat that the Imps received two red cards before half-time.

There was no identity under Nuno. West Ham are unbeaten on the road and won 1-0 at the then table-topping Swansea last month but it has been hard to tell Nuno broke the Football League transfer record with the £22m signing of the Belgium midfielder Arne Engels from Celtic. Even Jarrod Bowen, who was convinced to sign a new deal in the summer, has been off colour. Nuno’s tactics mean the winger, West Ham’s top scorer, is often crowded out.

West Ham were lopsided against West Brom. Enough was enough. Kretinsky, who is not at every game, was unimpressed when he attended West Ham’s 3-2 defeat by Southampton a week earlier. He pays attention to the views of Bowen, Tomas Soucek and Mark Noble, the technical director and former club captain.

Nuno, whose substitutions were almost as weird as his starting lineups, had lost the players. The mood darkened after the West Brom game. West Ham were easy to play through because of Nuno’s reluctance to use a holding midfielder, an issue exacerbated by his refusal to use Edson Álvarez or Soungoutou Magassa after both sought moves during the summer.

Magassa’s exile has caused disquiet. Not only is a young asset being devalued, a fragile defence is going without enough protection. West Ham have a lot of No 8s but they need a No 6. It is an area for Parker to address. He will also need to work out whether to stick with Mads Hermansen in goal, and the jury is out on summer signings.

One source questions whether West Ham targeted players equipped to handle the intensity of the Championship. Divine Mukasa, the 19-year-old midfielder, is talented but inconsistent. Manor Solomon and Edvin Austbø have flattered to deceive on the left wing. Joël Veltman, the 34-year-old Dutch right-back, has had fitness issues. Adama Boiro, a 24-year-old left‑back on loan from Athletic Bilbao, has not been seen since a cameo against Derby in early September. The three strikers signed by Nuno across two windows have toiled; Pablo Felipe, Taty Castellanos and Joël Piroe have five league goals between them this season.

Nils Koppen, the head of recruitment appointed in the summer, will have to be busy in January, but Parker will hope to have made his impact before the window opens. He is not known for expansive football but he is proven at this level. Parker won promotion with Bournemouth, Burnley and Fulham. The 46-year-old’s track record is clear and it helps that he has an association with West Ham.

Parker, whose all-action playing style made him a fan favourite, knows how difficult it can be in east London. He played in some pretty bad West Ham sides, experienced relegation in 2011 and arrives with the club in a tricky spot again.

It is not the moment to start worrying about Parker’s questionable record as a Premier League manager. What do West Ham do if they go up? Do they stick with Parker? Do they make an instant change? Well, how about they get promoted first? The rest can wait.

#873. Steinmeier in China: A major state visit in uncertain times

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is traveling to China on a state visit in a period of political and economic uncertainty. Germany is seeking alternative partners in the region but also wants good ties with Beijing.

Eight years have passed since Frank-Walter Steinmeier's last trip to China. Since then, the relationship between China and Europe has changed significantly. The German president plans to spend several days touring China before concluding his visit in Beijing, where he will meet with China's leaders.

His visit comes just as the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee is convening for its plenary session, a major annual event that foreign dignitaries usually avoid when timing their visits.

The focus of the president's five-day trip will be "Germany's diverse and complex relations with China, as well as the challenges involved," his office said in a statement. In addition to sites of cultural exchange, the itinerary will also include a visit to a Volkswagen plant in Hefei.

The automotive industry, in particular, illustrates the dilemma facing Germany's China policy. China is one of the most important markets for German automotive and machinery manufacturers, as well as for the chemical industry. At the same time, state-supported overcapacity in China is putting pressure on European manufacturers.

Not only that. Germany and Europe are dependent on China for raw materials and technologies, which means they are increasingly seeking out alternative partnerships.

Steinmeier was once an advocate of the policy of "change through trade" — the idea that other countries could be persuaded to become more democratic with the leverage of global trade — which has few adherents left in Germany today.

Now he must now pursue a tougher European line in Beijing. Caught between partnership and competition, Europe leaders recently managed to reach an agreement: Imports of plug-in hybrid vehicles from China are to be scaled back.

"That was a concrete step, but it can only be the beginning," said Michael Laha, an expert on China at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) in Berlin.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Coinciding with Steinmeier's state visit to China, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is traveling to the Indo-Pacific with business representatives. His visit to Japan, Singapore and South Korea will focus on competitiveness, technological upheavals, defense cooperation and critical raw materials. Merz is visiting companies and attending important regional economic conferences in Tokyo and Seoul.

The dual trips are Berlin's attempt to send a twofold message: While the chancellor is "deliberately strengthening Germany's partnerships in the Indo-Pacific at a time of global upheaval," according to Laha, the president is seeking dialogue with Beijing at a time when Germany and Europe are recalibrating their relationship with China.

"This joint trip sends a very well-coordinated message to the Chinese that we remain committed to the partnership but at the same time are taking steps to reduce risk," said Laha, before adding that this is a difficult balancing act that also allows China to save face.

While Merz will be accompanied by a large economic delegation, Steinmeier will be traveling to China with representatives from German culture, politics, and academia. Mikko Huotari, director of the China Institute MERICS, is also expected to be part of the delegation — even though Beijing has imposed sanctions on the institute. "The fact that he is coming along sends a clear message to the Chinese side that we do not approve of the sanctions," said Laha.

In 2021, the EU imposed sanctions against several Chinese party and regional officials, as well as an organization accused of serious human rights violations and oppressing the Uyghur minority. It was the first time such sanctions had been imposed on China since the Tiananmen Square massacre in 1989, and Beijing did not take kindly to them. In response, the Chinese government imposed entry bans and other sanctions against European politicians, scholars, and institutions, including MERICS.

Laha did not expect human rights to play a major role in the German president's trip. Steinmeier is considered a pragmatist when it comes to China policy. As foreign minister, he distanced himself from his predecessor Joschka Fischer, a critic of China, and even criticized Chancellor Angela Merkel when she hosted the Dalai Lama.

On the subject of Ukraine, Steinmeier is likely to be more direct and raise the issue of China's role in the conflict. "Beijing is clearly on Moscow's side," said Laha. In Berlin, however, officials are convinced that China can do more to persuade Russia to engage in serious negotiations and find a solution to the conflict.

Steinmeier may make this clear in his speech at Peking University on Thursday. Germany has "long viewed China's emergence with respect and goodwill," read a statement from the president's office. Today, however, the focus is less on China's continued rise and more on how it uses its growing power.

"If the president points out that Russia used its power to attack a sovereign state, he could be alluding to another regional connection: Taiwan," said Laha. That could be seen as an appeal to Beijing to assume more responsibility for the regional and international order.

To conclude his visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership in Beijing. Talks are planned with President Xi Jinping, whom he has known for nearly two decades, as well as with Premier Li Qiang and the chairman of the National People's Congress, Zhao Leji.

The trip marks the culmination of Steinmeier's focus on Asia during his second term in office. Since then, he has deliberately sought to forge close ties with partners in the region and has advocated for greater diversification. Now China, which is Germany's most important and most challenging partner, will come to its own conclusion.

This article was originally published in German.

#872. Craig Melvin Confronts Martha Stewart After Halloween Controversy

Martha Stewart and Craig Melvin reunited on Today so the lifestyle guru could express her regrets for blaming the host for her “stupid” decision to dress like a homeless person on Halloween.

Martha Stewart is serving up some more accountability for her actions.

After the Martha Stewart Living founder blamed Craig Melvin for her dressing as a homeless person for Halloween, claiming that her decision came from the Today anchor accidentally spilling chocolate on her during the Oct. 30 episode, she addressed those comments with the veteran journalist.

"It was Saturday, and it was Halloween, and I was invited to a party," Stewart recalled to Melvin on the Nov. 6 episode of the morning show. "I was very busy all day doing a lot of gardening. We're planting lots of trees up at the farm, and I really hadn't planned a Halloween costume this year."

Though she emphasized that she usually does very "elaborate costumes," she said she "didn't have a costume" because Melvin—who was dressed as her BFF Snoop Dogg for Today's beloved Halloween episode—dropped chocolate ganache on her white sweater as they learned to decorate a themed cheesecake.

"I don't blame you at all," Stewart asserted. "It was a joke that I said I blamed you. It was stupid. It was tone deaf."

Meanwhile, Melvin was ready for clarification on his alleged role in this mess.

"I was making a joke," the lifestyle guru emphasized. "I was giving a talk, and I just made a joke that you had spilled chocolate on me, and so I couldn't wear that costume, which I had planned to wear on Halloween night to this party."

Even so, Melvin made sure to emphasize that he had no involvement in Stewart's costume controversy.

He added, "To be clear, there was no connection between that and the costume later."

As for what lessons the 85-year-old learned?

"Pay closer attention to social issues," she reflected. "I'm aware of all those social issues, as you can imagine, and I care desperately about all the problems facing us, but I made a mistake. I was stupid. What else can I say?"

"I'm so sorry," she continued. "I hope that my followers and my fans and the rest of America forgive me for doing something that was not meant in any way to be a bad thing."

But it wasn't just online critics slamming Stewart's costume. In fact, she admitted her 14-year-old grandson Truman told her it was "tone deaf" after she sent him a photo of the look.

"I apologized because I was not making fun of anybody or making light of the great problems that face our country," she added. "I certainly hope our new administration takes big steps to repair a lot of the damage that's being done, and the poor and the hungry and everyone else is taken care of better."

Before suggesting Melvin was behind her costume, Stewart expressed remorse and asserted that the homelessness issue in the U.S. is close to her heart.

"Homelessness continues to remain one of America's greatest challenges and ongoing crises," she said in a separate statement to People on Nov. 1, "something that I care deeply about and I have spent a significant amount of time and effort supporting charities that combat this ongoing social epidemic."

Before the debacle, however, she and Melvin had a spooktacular time on Today's Halloween episode. Keep reading to see the costumes worn by the other cohosts.

#870. ‘She can do what Beckham did’: Océane Hurtré making waves at Birmingham

WSL’s second-highest goalscorer is likened to England legend for her crossing and has earned France call-up

At the conclusion of Birmingham’s warm-up, the players quietly and carefully placed their footballs into a draw-string bag. All except one, Océane Hurtré, who nonchalantly chipped hers straight into the bag from about 15 yards. It was an innocuous moment that might have escaped most onlookers at Hednesford Town’s Keys Park but it demonstrated the swagger with which she is playing.

To observe the 22-year-old warming up before the 1-1 League Cup draw at Aston Villa last week was to witness a player making skills look easy, taking one touch where others took two and pulling off no-look passes. She is backing up that panache in the Women’s Super League, as the joint second-highest goalscorer with six from the promoted side’s opening eight matches. Only Khadija Shaw has scored more.

Add in two WSL assists and a goal and an assist on her France debut last month and it has been a breakthrough campaign for Hurtré that very few expected, except perhaps those who followed closely her career in France. They include the former France head coach Olivier Echouafni, who gave a 16-year-old Hurtré her professional debut for Paris Saint-Germain during the title-winning 2020-21 campaign, the only time a side have stopped OL Lyonnes from finishing top in the past 20 years.

“She listens to everything the coach says, she’s very attentive, she’s very focused,” Echouafni says. “She’s like a sun, because when you speak with her there’s a big light. She was always quite skilful, moving the ball quickly to draw out her opponent, and had a good shot and delivered quality crosses.

“Back then, she lacked athletic stamina, the ability to sustain repeated bursts and sometimes also struggled in one-on-one situations because she was so young, but she has made great progress since then. She has also made great progress mentally – her move to Birmingham has done her a world of good.”

WSL fans are enjoying Hurtré’s pace, skill and general attacking threats, but imprinted in Echouafni’s memory are her defensive efforts as a youngster. He recalls Hurtré, on her second league appearance, against Paris FC in May 2021, replacing the Canada full-back Ashley Lawrence with two minutes remaining. “She cleared the ball off the goalline and prevented the equaliser,” he says. “It was a very important action because, one week later, PSG won the championship.”

To describe her as surrounded by experienced professionals at PSG would be a big understatement. When she had made her debut, in Europe against the Polish side Gornik Leczna, she was on the same team as a 42-year-old Formiga. Her gratitude to PSG is clear: she was spotted at the Joie Stadium last week watching Manchester City take on PSG in the Women’s Champions League, sitting just above her former club’s bench. PSG loaned Hurtré to Dijon in 2022 to gain more first-team experience and to Bordeaux in 2023-24. An injury at each affected her game time but she left a strong impression.

“I wanted to sign Océane for two main reasons,” says Sylvain Carric, Dijon women’s general manager from 2022 until 2026, who now runs the Strasbourg women’s teams. “The first was, naturally, the quality of her left foot – it’s magnificent; she can put the ball exactly where she wants it. The second was her versatility. She’s capable of playing as a left-back, a winger or a No 8.

“Océane left a fantastic impression during her time at Dijon. She had the intelligence to come to Dijon to grow, rather than remaining on the bench at PSG. She was a very good player and an excellent teammate, always smiling. She has been supported by a very good inner circle, especially her father, who I believe played an important role in her success. As for her potential, it was obvious, especially given that left foot, but she just needed to adapt her physique for the elite level. Now that she’s brought all those elements together, I’m certainly not surprised.”

Hurtré took a risk when she joined second-tier Birmingham in the summer of 2025 but it has paid off after she helped them to win promotion and she has goals against clubs including Arsenal, Brighton and Manchester City.

Birmingham’s head coach, Amy Merricks, said last month: “We’re incredibly proud of her. I’m not going to share it but, if I did share where she was when she first came in, people wouldn’t quite believe the turnaround. There were so many areas that she needed support with, transitioning to a different country at a young age. She’s learned English, which is a massive step.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

“Everyone sees her work on the pitch but we are fortunate to see the amount of work she’s done of it, and it absolutely translates. She’s diligent, she’s a student of the game, and she thoroughly deserved the call-up [for France].”

Hurtré was rewarded for her strong start with the WSL player of the month award for September. Sylvain Jamet, a women’s football writer for the French magazine footofeminin, saw her play at the Under-20 Women’s World Cup in Costa Rica and believes Hurtré has become “a lot faster” at Birmingham.

“Her technical ability and her set-piece deliveries with her left foot stood out,” Jamet says of Hurtré’s six years representing France’s youth teams. “Since she’s arrived in the UK, they must have worked on her speed.”

Hurtré’s goal contributions in France’s 9-0 win against Latvia have boosted her hopes of a place at the World Cup next summer. Jamet, comparing her to Chelsea’s left-sided France player Sandy Baltimore, says: “They’re competing for the same place with France now. She’s less explosive than Sandy, but she’s better technically for the crosses and passing. Baltimore’s obviously fantastic, more like a one-v-one player, taking on defenders.

“Hurtré can cross from anywhere, she can do what [David] Beckham did, basically, crossing from deep, crossing from anywhere. She had very good first cap for France. There’s a good chance she will be in the squad for the World Cup. I really expect her to get one of those 26 places.”

#868. Has a footballer ever run a marathon faster than James Milner? | The Knowledge

Plus: managers sacked after signing new deals, war victims commemorated on kits and the first club website (part II)

Mail us with all of your questions and answers

It came as no surprise to the Knowledge that James Milner had spent the early months of his retirement training for – and then running in – the New York City Marathon. Yes, the bleep test-loving former Brighton, Liverpool and Manchester City player recorded an excellent time of 3hr 9min 4sec, an average of 7min 13sec per mile. Not bad for a 40-year-old whose physique is more like that of a wrestler than a whippet. “A few years ago, I feel like I could have definitely done sub-3:00,” he said, lamenting his late-career injuries for hindering him.

In 2012 we ran a column listing footballers’ fastest marathon times, with the former Leicester playmaker Muzzy Izzet leading the pack on 3hr 22min 36sec at the 2011 London Marathon. That very respectable time has now been surpassed by the Premier League’s record appearance maker, so we thought we had better take a gulp of our isotonic energy drink and run through a few more tales of football’s marathon men and women.

More recent marathon attempts by either active or former footballers puts Izzet down in 12th place, just behind André Schürrle, who clocked 3hr 21min 25sec in Berlin last year, though clearly wanted a greater challenge than a mere 26.2 miles. This year, the 35-year-old completed the 167.7-mile six-stage Marathon des Sables in 51hr 41min 16sec, placing 675th overall. He also climbed Mont Blanc. But back to marathons, where the fastest time we can find for a female footballer is 3hr 40min 30sec by the former USA midfielder Lauren Holiday. She is closely followed by her good friends from the USWNT, Leslie Osborne (3hr 41min 33sec) and Abby Wambach (3hr 44min 25sec).

The Fulham manager, Álvaro Arbeloa, is 11th on our overall list (3hr 15min 21sec, Valencia 2019), with Kevin Kilbane, who always looked like he had a marathon runner’s spring in his step, 10th on 3hr 14min 44sec (London, 2013). A tip of the hat now to Danny Mills, father to the GB Olympic runner George Mills, with Mills Sr running the 2023 London Marathon in 3hr 12min 18sec at 45 years of age. Meanwhile, Milner’s run places him eighth as we approach some of football’s more serious runners.

The former Dundee United and West Ham defender Christian Dailly clocked a seriously impressive 3hr 6min 26sec at the 2013 London Marathon. “In 1990, I went from boys’ football in May to my Dundee United debut in August,” said Dailly after the race. “We’d be down at the beach, and all of a sudden, I’d be running through the sea at St Andrews or up and down the sand dunes. When I got to pre-season at Dundee United, I was flying, running away from everyone.” Dailly went into athletics coaching when his football career ended. We did not expect a goalkeepeer to be jostling for position towards the front of the pack, but the former Derby County and Sheffield Wednesday stopper Lee Grant hared around London in 3hr 0min 33sec this year.

And so we get to the hallowed ground of a sub-three hour marathon and a select group of only five. The Real Madrid legend Raúl González was clearly being cheered from the rafters as he ran his home marathon in 2hr 59min 22sec in 2019. “It was only the second marathon of my life. I wanted to break three hours, and I’m very happy with what I’ve accomplished,” he said. The Oxford United manager, Aaron Ramsey, used his relative youth at 35 to tear up the Stockholm Marathon this summer in exactly 2hr 59min. Arjen Robben was known for his blistering pace over short distances in his glittering career but he showed that he could blend speed with stamina as he raced round Rotterdam in 2023 in a time of 2hr 58min 33sec.

Before setting out on his managerial career, Luis Enrique trained like a demon for the Florence Marathon, with his hard work paying off as he came home in 2hr 58min 8sec. He has since continued his fitness regime, competing in the Frankfurt Ironman event and the Marathon des Sables.

But the gold medal for the fastest former footballer to run a marathon goes to Alexei Smertin. The former Chelsea and Russia utility man took endurance running seriously when he retired in 2008 and hit a peak of 2hr 48min 17sec at the Kazan Marathon in 2020, aged 45. That is an incredible pace of 6min 25sec per mile. He has since tried switching to longer distances as he has aged but believes he may still have one or two quick marathons left in him. “I’ve been leaning toward ultras. One reason is that speed declines with age,” he said recently. “I thought I’d never be able to improve my personal best [2:48:17] … [but] I have a few more years to improve my speed.”

“What is the soonest a manager has been sacked after signing a contract extension?” asks Dave Smythe.

Adam Clark comes in hot with the first suggestion: “Leam Richardson, then of Wigan Athletic, signed a three-year contract extension on 25 October 2022 and was sacked 16 days later on 10 November 2022. Wigan then recruited Kolo Touré on a three-and-a-half year contract, who subsequently lasted just nine games.”

“I’m pretty sure when Watford sacked Glenn Roeder in 1996 he’d signed a contract extension about a fortnight earlier?” suggests Daz Pearce. Good shout, Daz: Watford were not yet in their era of sacking a manager every month, but Roeder – initially appointed at Vicarage Road in 1993 – was given the boot by Watford just 10 days after signing a new one-year contract extension in February 1996. “I am sure I have learned from this experience,” said Roeder, who announced his intention to stay in the game. He would not get another managerial job for another five years, enjoying a successful stint at West Ham from 2001-03.

Not a contract extension but Kevin Cullis’s appointment at Swansea City in 1996 lasted just seven days. Cullis, who never played professionally, had only ever previously coached non-league Crawley Town’s youth team and was later jailed for fraud in 2003, and didn’t get off to the best start in Wales with Swans players reportedly ignoring his tactics at half-time against Blackpool during just his second game in charge. Cullis resigned shortly afterwards.

Elsewhere, Dave Bassett lasted less than four days at Crystal Palace in 1984, Marcelo Bielsa resigned as manager of Lazio after just two days in the job in 2016 and Leroy Rosenior’s 10-minute stint at Torquay United is Knowledge folklore. You can read more about that here.

We have received some new responses to last week’s Knowledge archive, which features some 2016 answers to the question: who were the first football club to have an official website?

“Last week, Martyn Amos reported an Ipswich fan website started in 1990,” wrote a sceptical Alan Terlep (and others), “but history records that the first known website went online in August 1991, so if that’s correct he has a claim to fame well beyond the Knowledge. A fan site that was already active in 1993 may well be the oldest or there though.”

Fellow reader Mark Francome, who works at a global IT service provider so should know a thing or two about this, emails that “Luton Town fans had ‘WHOSH’ (‘Worldwide Hatters On The Super Highway’), which dates from 1994,” while “Millwall also had ‘You’ll Never Make The Station’ from around the same time. No records exist to confirm the internet rumour that Millwall admins hacked their Luton counterparts and ripped up the HTML.”

“Portsmouth’s new kit has names of fallen soldiers on it. Are there other examples of clubs recognising war victims on their kit?” asked Simon Cook in August 2014.

Andrew Walker points us towards Raith Rovers’ away kit for the 2014-15 season, which has been designed to pay tribute to the 16th Royal Scots regiment, a battalion formed of sportsmen, seven of whom came from the Kirkcaldy club. Three Rovers players – Jimmy Todd, Jimmy Scott and George McLay – were killed during the conflict.

“We wanted to do something completely different for next season in terms of kit colours,” the Raith chair, Turnbull Hutton, told the Dundee Courier,” but at the same time the board has been considering a suitable way to mark this centenary in an appropriate manner, so we have brought these two ambitions together with our new green and black strip. “We hope that it captures the imagination of the Scottish footballing public and, through next season’s sports pages, that it ensures that we really do remember the sacrifices of our players and so many others 100 years ago.”

And in Wales, Aberystwyth Town are also commemorating the 100th anniversary of the outbreak of the first world war. “We’re the kit suppliers to Aberystwyth Town Football Club in the Welsh Premier League,” write the good folk at RM Teamwear, “and this season we produced their home strip honouring the centenary of the first world war, more specifically on the sleeves we have the names of players who played for the club and lost their lives in the Great War. Their name, rank and regiment are on players 1-14 in the war veteran player’s position he used to play. Others have “In Memory of Players of This Club Who Fell in the Great War” as seen in the attached photo.”

“Not only were Rangers v Dundee United and Manchester City v Barnsley in 2004-05 the only British league matches to finish 7-1 that season, the same opposing goalkeepers also played in both matches,” flags Stephen Toal. “Ronald Waterreus played for Rangers and Manchester City while Nick Colgan turned out for both Dundee United and Barnsley. Are there any other examples of opposing goalkeepers coming up against each other twice in the same season for a different set of opposing teams?”

“Following Coventry City’s 3-1 victory over Sunderland, I noticed a potentially unique statistic involving Luke O’Nien, who has now played in defeats against Coventry in all four divisions of English league football. Is this a first?” ponders Kirk Savage.

“Has ever been a headed goal awarded goal of the season?” wonders Rupert Sheard. “I can think of a few belters, but awards tend to go to ones kicked in.”

“Which club team has had the most international captains playing together at one time?” asks MH Zahid. “Conversely, which international team has had the most club captains in its starting lineup at one time?”

#867. Toothbrush zaps bacteria with electricity that’s made when bristles move

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The history of the manual toothbrush has been traced back to the tenth-century Tang Dynasty in China. Credit: Valentyna Yeltsova/Getty

Researchers at Peking University in Beijing have developed a toothbrush in which bacteria are destroyed not only by mechanical friction, but also through an electrical charge that is generated by brushing. The work was published in Science Advances on 4 November1.

Generating electricity through brushing is a “new twist on an old concept”, says Frank Scannapieco, a periodontist at the University at Buffalo in New York. It might reduce plaque more efficiently than do conventional manual toothbrushes, although more tests are needed to prove efficacy and safety, he says.

The researchers showed that the brush did not damage the surface of the teeth and was not toxic to human cells, but they did not look at long-term safety or cost.

Bristled toothbrushes — which humans have used in various forms since the tenth century ad — rely mainly on motion to manually disrupt plaque, the film of bacteria, saliva and food particles that forms around teeth.

The team made the bristles from polyvinylidene fluoride, a polymer that they stretched and heated to obtain a piezoelectric form — meaning that it generated a charge when deformed.

When used to scrub teeth, the bending bristles release charges that create highly reactive forms of oxygen in nearby saliva. These molecules damage the cell membranes of bacteria in the plaque, say the researchers. When the bristles relax, the material reabsorbs the charges.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03586-y

Lu, Y. et al. Sci. Adv. 12, eaeg5744 (2026).

#866. What Germany thinks of carmaker Audi's $4 billion deal with Trump

The luxury carmaker is set to open its first factory in the United States — a move Trump credits to his tariffs. DW examines the German reaction amid a massive auto industry cull at home.

US President Donald Trump announced the investment on Saturday, during a campaign rally in Georgia, a key battleground state for his Republican Party in the midterm elections next week.

Audi quickly confirmed the plan, saying it would build its first US factory near Macon, Georgia, costing around $4 billion (€3.6 billion) and creating some 4,500 jobs.

The German automaker said construction would begin next year, with a planned annual production of up to 200,000 vehicles due to start in the early 2030s.

The firm plans to build premium SUVs for the US market at the plant, marking a "long-term commitment" to what it said was "one of the world's most important premium markets."

The US investment comes as German automakers face unprecedented pressure from China, rising costs and two conflicts.

Backed by huge government subsidies, Chinese rivals have stolen a march in the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), scaling up production of new models that are fast gaining market share in a crowded global auto market.

BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Audi's parent company, Volkswagen— the world's second-largest automaker — have all issued profit warnings in recent months as margins come under pressure.

They've also announced major cost-cutting. VW is preparing to axe up to 100,000 jobs by 2030, while Audi's factory in Neckarsulm, which has around 15,000 staff, is one of four plants at risk of closure.

Trump credited his 15% tariffs on European-made vehicles for Audi's investment, saying it "would not have happened without tariffs."

While the commitment does feed into Trump's plan to bring manufacturing back to the United States from abroad, Audi said it was making the huge outlay for growth and resilience.

“We have much greater ambitions for Audi in America," said the carmaker's CEO Gernot Döllner, who appeared alongside Trump at the Republican's campaign rally.

"The United States is one of the world's most important premium markets, and we have not yet realized our full potential. We are determined to change that ... This is about building a stronger Audi business in America — not only about building a factory," he said.

However, Trump's tariffs have undoubtedly added to the automaker's woes.

Audi, which currently exports to the US market from Europe and Mexico, said the additional costs amounted to about €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion) last year.

With more than 160,000 vehicles sold, Audi's US sales last year fell 16%, amid intense competition and after Trump scrapped subsidies on electric vehicles in its second-biggest market.

By building a US factory, Audi should be able to avoid or reduce Trump's tariffs, industry analysts say.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There's been fierce criticism of the deal due to the severe pressure facing German automakers and because the new US investment could mean further job losses at home.

Much of the criticism focused on Döllner's rally appearance alongside Trump.

The center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)'s transport policy spokesperson Isabel Cademartori described it as campaign assistance for an autocrat who is waging a trade war against Germany.

"This is a disgrace, especially considering the history of the Volkswagen Group," she stated, referring to the company's links with Adolf Hitler's Nazi party during World War II.

Christiane Benner, president of the powerful IG Metall union, labeled the rally appearance as "extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and not worthy of the company."

VW works council chief Daniela Cavallo went further, saying Döllner had let himself be turned "into a puppet in [Trump's] propaganda show."

Cavallo, however, noted that the US plant could make sense from a business perspective, as VW needs to grow its market share there.

An Audi spokesperson defended the US investment, saying it was "not a decision against Germany, but rather a step toward strengthening our global competitiveness."

Manfred Döss, chairman of Audi's supervisory board, insisted the automaker's future cannot be secured by cost-cutting and efficiency alone.

"We need the courage to invest, to seize new opportunities and to make decisions that will shape our company for decades to come," he added.

The announcement certainly appears timed to coincide with the US midterm elections on November 3.

Voters will decide whether the Republicans or Democrats hold the balance of power in Congress during Trump's last two years in office.

Holding the announcement in the key battleground state of Georgia is seen as a strategic move to boost the fortunes of local Republican candidates.

Since he returned to the White House last year, Trump has used tariffs and political pressure to force global automakers to relocate their factories to American soil.

Audi's investment follows moves by Stellantis and Japan's Toyota to expand US production, while Honda is in talks to build a new US plant.

US auto giants General Motors and Ford have also promised to increase domestic production.

While one investment announcement may not be enough to sway many voters, it serves one of Trump's main election promises — to revive industrial production in the US.

#864. Meghan Markle's Dad Thomas Markle Arrested in Child Pornography Case

Thomas Markle Sr., the father of Meghan Markle, was arrested by the FBI on Nov. 6 in Florida on suspicion of possessing child sex abuse materials. He previously denied the allegations.

The investigation into Thomas Markle is coming to a head.

The father of Meghan Markle was arrested on Nov. 6 by the FBI in Florida on suspicion of possessing child sex abuse materials, the U.S. Attorney's Office confirmed in a release. He is expected to make his first appearance in court the same day.

According to the statement shared online, Thomas allegedly possessed materials which included "sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls," in two storage units he rented in the Los Angeles area since 2008. He’s been charged with one count of possession of child pornography. If convicted, per the statement, Thomas would face a maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.

“Mr. Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayl. “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

The 82-year-old’s arrest reportedly occurred at the Florida care home he’d been living in since he underwent a leg amputation in December 2025, per the The Sun, citing footage obtained at the scene. A wheelchair-bound Thomas could be seen in handcuffs in photos published by the outlet.

E! News has attempted to locate a rep or attorney for Thomas for comment but was unable to do so.

Thomas’ arrest comes mere weeks after his son Thomas Markle Jr., Meghan’s half-brother, accused their father of possessing child sex abuse materials, which he said he found in his house in the Philippines.

Thomas, however, soon denied all the allegations.

“I'm shocked, I'm hurt and I'm very upset that my son is making these accusations against me,” he told The Daily Mail on Oct. 23. “I could never do what I'm being accused of. It's the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”

He added, “This is bulls--t. It's just a bunch of lies. It's sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

His daughter Samantha Markle, who has been his caretaker in Florida, also slammed the allegations.

“There is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever and my brother is disgusting for making them up,” Samantha added to the outlet. “He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”

At the time, the FBI confirmed its involvement in the investigation into Thomas, noting it would “provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law.”

As for Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex—who shares two children with husband Prince Harry—shared she was “deeply distressed” over the allegations in a statement with E! News, noting her thoughts were with “any children who may have been harmed.”

The 45-year-old also shared insight into what information she’d been made privy to previously.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection,” she explained. “That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.”

Though she didn’t specify he allegations, she noted they’re a large reason she’s been estranged from Thomas in recent years.

“I hope it can now be understood that despite certain media publications' distortion over the years,” she said, “any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.”

As for now, she hopes justice can be served.

“The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” Meghan concluded. “The priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”

(E! and MS NOW are both part of Versant Media family.)
